content_voiceover: This slide compiles three past board questions on coagulation physiology, exactly the style you'll face on your exam. Question A, from year 111, question 39, asks which hemostatic protein concentrations are reduced by L-asparaginase treatment, listing antithrombin, protein C, protein S, fibrinogen, and t-PA. Classic teaching is that L-asparaginase, used in ALL therapy, suppresses hepatic protein synthesis broadly, but the two proteins most consistently and clinically emphasized are antithrombin and fibrinogen, which is choice one plus four, answer A. Question B, numbered 46, asks which coagulation factors are activated directly by thrombin, listing factor five, factor thirteen, factor eleven, and factor one, fibrinogen. Thrombin is a promiscuous enzyme: beyond cleaving fibrinogen to fibrin, it directly activates factor five, factor eight, factor eleven, and factor thirteen. All four listed factors, five, thirteen, eleven, and fibrinogen, are indeed direct thrombin substrates, so the answer is all of them, choice B. Question C, from year 110, question 59, asks you to identify the incorrect statement about activated protein C. It correctly degrades FVa and FVIIIa, and FV Leiden causes resistance to APC, and APC still requires protein S as a cofactor, all true statements. The false statement is that APC degrades thrombomodulin, APC does not degrade thrombomodulin, thrombomodulin is the receptor on endothelium that helps activate protein C in the first place, so that's the incorrect answer, choice C.
keypoints: L-asparaginase classically reduces antithrombin and fibrinogen levels
Thrombin directly activates factors V, VIII, XI, and XIII, plus converts fibrinogen to fibrin
Activated protein C degrades FVa and FVIIIa and requires protein S as cofactor
APC does NOT degrade thrombomodulin, that's the false statement to catch
keypoint_voiceover: Quick recap of these three questions: L-asparaginase drops antithrombin and fibrinogen; thrombin directly activates factors five, eight, eleven, thirteen, and fibrinogen; and activated protein C degrades FVa and FVIIIa with protein S as its cofactor, but it never degrades thrombomodulin, that's the trap answer.
